title: From Spain to Egypt: How Eclipse Chasing Became One of Travel's Most Devoted Subcultures
excerpt: The August 12 total solar eclipse over northern Spain drew thousands of astro-tourists from around the world, and the community is already planning for a six-minute totality in Luxor next year.
body:
• The August 12, 2026 total solar eclipse — the first visible in mainland Europe this century — drew eclipse chasers from across the globe to northern Spain, though wildfires in parts of the viewing path complicated travel plans.
  • Eclipse chasing has evolved from a niche scientific pursuit into a growing travel subculture, with dedicated enthusiasts planning trips years in advance around celestial events.
  • The next major target is August 2, 2027, when a total eclipse over Egypt will produce six minutes and 22 seconds of totality in Luxor — the longest visible to humans until 2114.
  • Astro-tourism is expanding as a broader category, driven by the fact that 80 percent of Americans and a third of the global population can no longer see the Milky Way from home due to light pollution.

Spain's Eclipse Drew a Global Audience

On August 12, the moon's shadow swept across the Northern Hemisphere from Russia through Greenland and Iceland before cutting across northern Spain and clipping northeastern Portugal. It was the first total solar eclipse visible in mainland Europe since 1999, and it drew a devoted community of eclipse chasers who had been planning their trips since the last North American eclipse in April 2024.

The path of totality passed over northern Spain during the late afternoon, creating an unusual viewing dynamic. Because the eclipse occurred close to sunset, observers had to account for the sun's low angle — requiring advance scouting of sight lines, a complication that wasn't necessary during North America's overhead eclipse two years earlier. The timing also coincided with the peak of the Perseid meteor shower on August 12–13, offering a double celestial reward for travelers who stayed overnight in rural areas with dark skies.

Not everything aligned perfectly. Devastating wildfires still burning in parts of Spain where the eclipse was visible forced some travelers to reconsider their plans. Elizabeth Warning, a TV researcher from Sydney who has chased eclipses across multiple continents, told AFP she considered canceling. "It's very sad," she said, adding that as an Australian well-versed in bushfire threats, her heart went out to the affected communities.

The Psychology of Chasing Totality

What drives people to spend thousands of dollars and travel to remote corners of the world for an event that lasts, at most, a few minutes?

"A total eclipse is not something you see, it's something you experience. The temperature drops, the light and the shadows are all in the wrong place, the colors are muted, there's a 360-degree sunset, the animals go to sleep — these things you cannot convey through a picture or a video."

— Ryan Milligan, Solar Physicist, Queen's University Belfast

Milligan has traveled to 12 different eclipses, reaching locations as far-flung as Siberia, Chile and the Faroe Islands. The experience, chasers say, is less visual spectacle than full-body phenomenon: the temperature drops several degrees in seconds, stars and planets appear in the daytime sky, birds fall silent, and a 360-degree sunset rings the horizon.

The community is small but tight-knit. Because everyone converges on the same narrow strip of land at the same time, chance encounters are common. Solar physicist Lucie Green of University College London described bumping into Milligan while driving through extremely remote northwestern Australia during a 2019 eclipse. Jenny Winker, a 60-year-old retiree from St. Paul, Minnesota, traveled to northern Spain with nine family members for the August 12 event.

The pursuit comes with a constant adversary: clouds. Green traveled all the way to Antarctica in 2021 only to see nothing. "I've got about a two-thirds success rate," she said. Warning described how clouds parted at the last second in the Faroe Islands in 2015, revealing the eclipse to her while observers just hundreds of meters away missed it entirely.

Next Stop: Six Minutes in Egypt

Eclipse chasers are already focused on August 2, 2027, when a total eclipse will pass over North Africa and the Middle East. In Luxor, home to the Valley of the Kings, totality will last six minutes and 22 seconds — the longest visible to humans until 2114. That duration, roughly triple what Spain offered, is expected to make the 2027 eclipse one of the most heavily attended celestial events in history.

Accommodation in Luxor and along the Egyptian path of totality is already being booked. Scientific American and other organizations are planning guided eclipse tours. Seasoned chasers recommend booking early and choosing refundable options — weather forecasts can shift viewing plans at the last minute, and the ability to relocate within the path of totality is often the difference between witnessing the event and staring at clouds.

A Broader Shift Toward Astro-Tourism

Eclipse chasing is the sharpest edge of a broader trend. Astro-tourism — traveling to dark-sky locations for meteor showers, aurora viewing, stargazing and other celestial events — is growing as urban light pollution makes the night sky invisible to an increasing share of the global population. According to research cited by the University of Southern California, 80 percent of Americans and one-third of the world's population can no longer see the Milky Way from their homes.

National parks, remote observatories and certified dark-sky sites have capitalized on the demand, offering guided stargazing programs and astronomy festivals. For the Indian diaspora, the 2027 Egypt eclipse offers a relatively accessible opportunity — direct flights from major Indian and Gulf cities to Cairo and Luxor make it far easier to reach than previous eclipse paths through Siberia, Antarctica or the remote Pacific.

As Warning put it with a laugh: "It's a very expensive, very odd addiction." But for the growing ranks of astro-tourists, the next fix is always just one eclipse away.
